chapters.title: Chapter 2: Ito Calculus: The Rules for Working With Randomness

lessons.title: From Deterministic to Stochastic Differential Equations

children.text: Round two of Rohan's interview starts with the interviewer writing a plain ordinary differential equation on the whiteboard, the kind from any first engineering course, and then, without a word, adding one extra term at the end. "That's it," the interviewer says. "That one extra term is the entire jump from deterministic modeling to everything you do on a trading desk." This lesson makes that one extra term precise, and gives you the object, the stochastic differential equation, that every model for the rest of this course is written in.

body.text: A stochastic differential equation is an ordinary differential equation with one added ingredient: a random shock built from a Wiener process. dX = a(X,t) dt + b(X,t) dW says the change in X over an instant is a deterministic drift plus a random term scaled by a diffusion coefficient. Nearly every model in modern quantitative finance, including the one behind the Black-Scholes formula, is a stochastic differential equation of exactly this shape.

children.text: Recap: What an Ordinary Differential Equation Says

An ordinary differential equation, or ODE, describes how a quantity X changes over time using a rule that depends only on X's current value and the current time, with no randomness anywhere in it. Given a starting value X(0), an ODE has exactly one solution, a single deterministic function of time. Run it twice with the same starting point and you get the exact same curve both times.

body.latex: \frac{dX}{dt} = a(X, t) \qquad \text{equivalently written as} \qquad dX = a(X,t)\, dt
body.caption: An ordinary differential equation: purely deterministic

children.text: Adding Randomness: The General Stochastic Differential Equation

A stochastic differential equation, or SDE, keeps the deterministic term and adds a second term built from a Wiener process. The function a(X,t) is called the drift, it is the deterministic trend the process would follow with no randomness at all. The function b(X,t) is called the diffusion coefficient, it controls how strongly the random Wiener increment shakes the process at each instant.

body.caption: The general form of an Ito stochastic differential equation

children.text: Why "dX/dt" Doesn't Actually Make Sense Here

markDefs.definition: A rigorously defined integral of a random process with respect to a Wiener process, denoted ∫b(X_s,s) dW_s. It replaces the ordinary Riemann integral wherever dW appears, since dW/dt does not exist as an ordinary function.

children.text: Chapter 1's third lesson proved that a Wiener process has no derivative anywhere, so dW(t)/dt is not a function you can plug numbers into. That means dX(t) = a\,dt + b\,dW is notation, not a literal division. The rigorous statement underneath it is an integral equation, where the second integral, called an

, is built directly, term by term, rather than by first differentiating W and then integrating. This course does not construct that integral from first principles; instead, it works with SDEs the way practitioners do, through Ito's lemma in the next two lessons and through direct simulation, which is exactly what the rest of this lesson sets up.

body.latex: X(t) = X(0) + \int_0^t a(X(s), s)\, ds \; + \; \int_0^t b(X(s), s)\, dW(s)
body.caption: The rigorous, integral form of the SDE above

children.text: Simulating an SDE: The Euler-Maruyama Method

You have already been simulating SDEs since Chapter 1, just without the formal name. The standard way to discretize any SDE numerically is the Euler-Maruyama method: chop time into small steps of size Δt, and at each step add the drift's contribution plus a random Wiener increment scaled by the diffusion coefficient. It is the direct stochastic analogue of Euler's method for ordinary differential equations, with one extra piece bolted on.

body.latex: X_{i+1} = X_i + a(X_i, t_i)\, \Delta t \; + \; b(X_i, t_i)\, \sqrt{\Delta t}\; Z_i, \qquad Z_i \sim N(0,1) \text{ i.i.d.}
body.caption: The Euler-Maruyama discretization scheme

children.text: Apply this to Reliance Industries (RELIANCE), trading at an illustrative ₹2,900, with an illustrative expected annual return of 12% and annualized volatility of 22%. Converting both into absolute rupee terms for this arithmetic Brownian motion model: μ = 0.12 × ₹2,900 = ₹348 per year, and σ = 0.22 × ₹2,900 = ₹638 per √year.

body.caption: A generic Euler-Maruyama simulator, applied to Reliance Industries
body.code:
import numpy as np

def euler_maruyama(X0, drift, diffusion, T, n_steps):
    dt = T / n_steps
    X = np.zeros(n_steps + 1)
    X[0] = X0
    for i in range(n_steps):
        t = i * dt
        Z = np.random.normal(0, 1)
        X[i + 1] = X[i] + drift(X[i], t) * dt + diffusion(X[i], t) * np.sqrt(dt) * Z
    return X

X0 = 2900
mu_absolute = 0.12 * X0     # 348 rupees/year
sigma_absolute = 0.22 * X0  # 638 rupees/sqrt(year)

drift = lambda X, t: mu_absolute
diffusion = lambda X, t: sigma_absolute

path = euler_maruyama(X0, drift, diffusion, T=1.0, n_steps=252)
print(f"S(1 year) = {path[-1]:.2f}")

body.title: One simulated year of RELIANCE under arithmetic Brownian motion with drift

children.text: Verifying the Drift: A Quick Check

A single simulated path, like the one charted above ending near ₹3,260, is noisy. But average the year-end value across a large number of independently simulated paths, and that average should converge to the model's theoretical mean, X(0) + μT, since the accumulated Wiener noise averages out to zero across many independent runs while the drift term does not.

body.caption: Averaging 100,000 simulated paths to verify the drift
body.code:
n_sims = 100_000
endpoints = [euler_maruyama(X0, drift, diffusion, T=1.0, n_steps=252)[-1] for _ in range(n_sims)]

print(f"Simulated mean S(1 year):   {np.mean(endpoints):.2f}")
print(f"Theoretical mean, X0 + mu*T: {X0 + mu_absolute:.2f}")

# Typical output:
# Simulated mean S(1 year):   3251.37
# Theoretical mean, X0 + mu*T: 3248.00

body.text: Look closely at the Euler-Maruyama formula and Chapter 1's very first simulation function: they are the same update rule. Adding drift × Δt is the only new piece; the random term, diffusion × √Δt × Z, is exactly the scaled Wiener increment used since Lesson 1 of this course. Simulating an SDE was never a new skill, it was this same random-walk-plus-scaling logic with one deterministic term added on top.

Do not think of "solving" a stochastic differential equation the way you solve an ODE, as finding one deterministic formula that gives a single number for X(t). The solution to an SDE is itself a stochastic process, an entire random object with a full distribution at each time t, not a single curve. What Chapter 3 calls "solving" geometric Brownian motion means finding a formula for X(t) written in terms of W(t) and t, a formula that still has a random W(t) sitting inside it. Every simulated path in this lesson is just one sample drawn from that solution's distribution, never the whole answer by itself.

body.title: Identify the drift and diffusion
body.question: In the SDE dX = 0.05·X dt + 0.30 dW, what are the drift and diffusion functions?
options: There is no drift term in this equation, only diffusion
body.explanation: The drift is whatever multiplies dt, here 0.05·X, and the diffusion coefficient is whatever multiplies dW, here the constant 0.30. This particular equation has a drift proportional to the current level of X, but a constant, level-independent diffusion term, a hybrid that is neither pure arithmetic nor pure geometric Brownian motion.

body.title: Compute the theoretical mean at a shorter horizon
body.prompt: Using this lesson's Reliance Industries calibration (X0 = ₹2,900, μ = ₹348 per year), what is the theoretical mean of X(0.5), after just 6 months? (Use E[X(T)] = X0 + μT.)
body.explanation: E[X(T)] = X0 + μT = 2,900 + 348 × 0.5 = 2,900 + 174 = ₹3,074. The diffusion term contributes zero to the mean at any horizon, since Wiener increments have mean zero; it only ever affects the spread around this mean, never the mean itself.

cards.definition: An equation of the form dX = a(X,t)dt + b(X,t)dW, describing a process whose instantaneous change has a deterministic drift plus a random term scaled by a diffusion coefficient.
The deterministic trend term in an SDE; the rate of change the process would follow if all randomness were switched off.
The term in an SDE that scales the random Wiener increment, controlling how strongly randomness perturbs the process at each instant.
The standard numerical scheme for simulating an SDE, updating the process at each small time step by adding drift × Δt plus diffusion × √Δt × a standard normal draw.

points: A stochastic differential equation, dX = a(X,t)dt + b(X,t)dW, generalizes an ordinary differential equation by adding a random term built from a Wiener process.
Because dW/dt does not exist, an SDE is rigorously an integral equation, with a stochastic (Ito) integral standing in for the ordinary integral wherever dW appears.
The solution to an SDE is an entire stochastic process, not a single deterministic curve; each simulated path is one sample from its distribution.

The Euler-Maruyama method simulates any SDE by updating X at each small step with drift × Δt plus diffusion × √Δt × a standard normal draw, the same update rule used since Chapter 1, now with a drift term added.
Averaging many simulated endpoints recovers the theoretical mean, X0 + μT, confirming that the diffusion term contributes only spread, never a shift in the average.

The next lesson introduces Ito's lemma, the tool needed to correctly analyze a function of a process defined by an SDE, something the diffusion term's quadratic variation makes impossible to do with the ordinary chain rule.
